source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Review that lines up general dual-process theory (Type 1 fast, associative; Type 2 slow, working-memory bound) with creativity models that split idea generation from evaluation. Concludes a simple map (generation = Type 1, evaluation = Type 2) does not hold.
numbers: Main text 7,474 words. Published Thinking & Reasoning 21(1) 40-60.
quote: Both generative and evaluative creative processing modes involve elements that have been attributed to each of the dual processes of cognition.
limits: Conceptual review, no new data. Its own Table 1 maps the models by hand.
agent_relevance: Do not assign 'generate' to fast and 'evaluate' to slow in the schema. Both modes may need cheap and costly steps; the code decides the mode, the model fills the slot.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Divergent thinking can be effortful and deliberate (Type 2-like); convergent insight can arrive after unconscious incubation (Type 1-like). So divergent/convergent does not equal Type 1/Type 2.
numbers: Cites Ward (1994), Frankish (2010), Wallas (1926).
limits: Argument from the literature, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Mode label (generate vs judge) and effort level (cheap vs deliberate) are two separate dials.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Basadur's ideation-evaluation cycles: problem finding, problem solving and implementation each mix ideation and evaluation in different ratios. Problem finding is ideation-heavy; implementation is evaluation-heavy. People differ in how much they favour ideating over evaluating.
numbers: Basadur et al. 1982; Basadur 1995 (as described in the review).
limits: Secondhand description; primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The ratio of generate steps to judge steps should depend on the state (early framing: mostly generate; late: mostly verify). Fits a code-set budget per state.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Blind Variation and Selective Retention (Campbell 1960; Simonton): ideas are produced by blind variation, then the fittest are retained. The review lists problems, including that successive ideas are not unrelated, as BVSR assumes (Feinstein 2006; Nijstad & Stroebe 2006).
limits: BVSR has long-standing critics (Dasgupta 2004, Eysenck 1995, Gabora 2005-2011, Sternberg 1998, Weisberg 2004).
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not blind and not independent (guardrail G4). Selection must be done by code on a real check, not by taking the model's own favourite.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Finke, Ward & Smith Geneplore: a generate phase (retrieve, associate, synthesise pre-inventive structures) then an explore phase (find attributes, test function). Ward's 'path of least resistance': people copy features of known exemplars, e.g. imagined aliens get arms and legs.
numbers: Finke, Ward & Smith 1992; Ward 1994.
limits: Model described through the review. See the parallel Geneplore deep document for details.
agent_relevance: Generation defaults to the familiar. A code-triggered 'avoid the prototype' step is plausible, but only after a signal (G1).

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Howard-Jones (2002) Dual-State model and Gabora's Honing Theory align most cleanly with dual-process cognition: associative (defocused) thought generates, analytic (focused) thought refines, in iteration. The review says serial or parallel operation of the two modes is unresolved.
quote: Nijstad et al. (p43): 'our model is not applicable to situations in which creativity occurs spontaneously without intentional effort'.
limits: Review notes no study has timed shifts directly; proposes chronometric work and ACC activation as a marker.
agent_relevance: Mode switch as an explicit, loggable event. Our logs of switch points would be the kind of data the review says is missing.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Mismatch hazard: showing examples during the generative phase hurts output (Jansson & Smith 1991), and cycling between modes too fast can make people judge ideas before they have matured.
numbers: Jansson & Smith 1991 (as cited).
limits: Inference by the review authors, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Do not show the model prior answers or critiques during first-pass generation. Delay judging until the generation quota is met.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Neural candidate for the switch: the salience network (anterior insula, ACC; Menon & Uddin 2010) toggles between default mode network (generative) and central executive network (evaluative). Ellamil et al. (2012) complicate this: DMN and CEN were both active in evaluation, and the medial temporal lobe in generation.
limits: Network labels are mapped loosely; the review itself says the mapping to dual-process types is unclear.
agent_relevance: An external controller that toggles modes maps to our program that decides transitions. A loose analogy, not a design reason.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: The review reports that the dual-pathway model does not treat flexibility and persistence as competing, but a personal communication from Nijstad finds the two measures unrelated, and that people may become entrenched in one pathway over time.
limits: Personal communication, not citable data.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment in one mode is a risk: a program-level counter that forces a mode change after a fixed number of failed attempts in the same frame would guard against it.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Dual pathway to creativity model: originality comes from either (1) flexibility (many categories, broad associations, less executive control) or (2) persistence (deep systematic work in few categories, more executive control). An 'idea monitor' filters ideas entering working memory.
numbers: Chapter, European Review of Social Psychology 21, pp. 34-77.
limits: Model is for intentional creative work; it says nothing about spontaneous creativity.
agent_relevance: Two ways to get novelty: switch category (reframe) or go deeper in one (more samples within a frame). Code can choose which by a signal such as a repeated category.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Authors' own pooled correlations among ideation measures. Flexibility relates to originality (r=.34) more than within-category fluency does (r=.12). Flexibility and within-category fluency are uncorrelated (r=.01). Originality and feasibility are negatively correlated (r=-.42).
numbers: 20 studies, total N=2118. Fluency-flexibility r=.72 (k=17, N=1858); fluency-originality r=.22 (k=13, N=1699); flexibility-originality r=.34 (k=10, N=1439); wcf-originality r=.12 (k=10); originality-feasibility r=-.42 (k=8, N=610).
limits: Not a systematic search: only studies by the authors. Heterogeneity (Qw) significant for most pairs. Task lengths 4 to 20 minutes, four topics. Sowden et al. quote r=.36, but the table reads .34.
agent_relevance: Original ideas are less feasible, so a generate-only loop drifts toward the infeasible. Code-side checks must offset that.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Persistence test 1: a narrower topic raised originality. Rietzschel (2005, Study 4.3) gave students a broad or narrow ideation topic.
numbers: N=102 undergraduates, 20 minutes. Originality M=2.33 narrow vs 2.18 broad (5-point scale). Fluency-originality r=.28, p<.05, in narrow; r=-.06 ns in broad.
limits: Small mean difference (0.15 points). Instruction (relevance vs originality) was a second manipulation and was partialled out. Thesis data reported in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Constraining the frame and sampling many times inside it gave original ideas. Supports many attempts inside one frame before reframing.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Persistence test 2: priming a sub-topic raised the share and the originality of ideas in that sub-topic. Rietzschel et al. (2007b, Study 1) primed nutrition or sports within the health topic.
numbers: N=75 undergraduates, 10 minutes. Share of nutrition ideas vs originality of nutrition ideas r=.36 (p<.01); sports r=.61 (p<.001). Controls: no priming, politics priming. Hygiene condition dropped (too few ideas).
limits: One study, small N, undergraduates, one topic. The share-originality link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Seeding a category and then asking for more ideas in it is a code-controlled deepening move.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Persistence via personality: Personal Need for Structure helps fluency and originality only when Personal Fear of Invalidity is low, and the effect runs through within-category fluency, not flexibility. Study 2 replicated Study 1c with the same procedure.
numbers: Study 1c N=102; Study 2 N=240 replicated the PNS x PFI interaction for fluency, originality and within-category fluency, not flexibility. Mediation by within-category fluency was full.
limits: A strict idea monitor (high PFI) killed originality. Baron & Kenny mediation is weak by modern standards.
agent_relevance: A harsh judge hurts novelty. Our judge should be applied after the generation quota, not inside it.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Mood and the two pathways (De Dreu, Baas & Nijstad 2008). Activating moods raised fluency and originality. Anger raised within-category fluency; happiness raised flexibility, but that contrast was not significant in Study 1.
numbers: Study 1 N=58, 2x2 mood induction, 8 minutes. Means anger/sad/happy/relaxed: fluency 13.32/10.16/11.88/10.42; originality 2.73/2.06/2.77/2.26; flexibility 3.65/3.56/4.01/3.46; within-category fluency 3.64/2.85/2.96/3.01. Observed power for flexibility under .20. Study 4 N=546, mood measured, 8 minutes.
limits: The authors admit the flexibility prediction failed in Study 1 and blame power. Mood induction by autobiographical writing.
agent_relevance: Small evidence base for state effects. No direct equivalent of mood for a model.

source: Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel & Baas (2010) The dual pathway to creativity model
finding: Remote Associates Test and evaluation: Harkins (2001, 2006) found people who expected evaluation solved more easy RAT items but fewer hard ones, because they used a systematic per-word search. Hard items need flexible, broad search.
numbers: Qualitative summary in the chapter; numbers not given there.
limits: Secondhand within the chapter; primary not opened.
agent_relevance: Strict step-by-step search suits easy items and harms hard ones: a reason to switch to a broader reframing operator when systematic search stalls.

source: Barr (2014 thesis, Univ. Waterloo) Reasoned connections: complex creativity and dual-process theories of cognition
finding: Cross-domain (remote) analogies were hard under limited Type 2 conditions and took longer than within-domain ones. Short presentation selectively hurt cross-domain analogies.
numbers: Exp 1 N=41 after one exclusion, 120 A:B::C:D items. Cross-domain true analogies 52.6% (SD 20.5) vs within-domain 89.3% (SD 10.0), t(41)=11.28. Non-analogy rejection 64.0% within vs 80.2% cross.
limits: Student sample. Word analogies are a narrow proxy for creative connection.
agent_relevance: Remote connections need reasoned effort, not just free association. Fast generation alone is a weak route to far links.

source: Barr (2014 thesis, Univ. Waterloo) Reasoned connections: complex creativity and dual-process theories of cognition
finding: More time and capacity (Exp 2) improved cross-domain analogy accuracy more than within-domain, a selective effect.
numbers: Cross-domain 52.6% (Exp 1) to 64.6% (Exp 2), +12 points; within-domain 89.0% to 93.3%, +4.3 points. Mixed ANOVA main effects Experiment F(1,81)=11.66, Domain F(1,81)=285.26; the Experiment x Domain interaction was reported significant.
limits: Between-experiment comparison, different samples and parameters, not random assignment.
agent_relevance: More thinking budget helps most where the link is remote. A budget lever tied to distance of the link is defensible.

source: Barr (2014 thesis, Univ. Waterloo) Reasoned connections: complex creativity and dual-process theories of cognition
finding: Cueing analytic vs intuitive responding (Exp 4) gave no accuracy difference for true cross-domain analogies, which was the key prediction; within-domain items did better with the analytic cue. The author reports being surprised.
numbers: N=76. Cross-domain true analogies: analytic cue 69.9% (SD 16.6) vs intuitive cue 69.0% (SD 15.1), t<1. Within-domain analogies: 93.6% analytic vs 91.1% intuitive, t(75)=2.69, p<.01. Cross-domain non-analogies: intuitive cue 78.9% vs analytic cue 73.8%, t(75)=-2.63, p<.01 (the reverse direction).
limits: Thesis result, partly a failed prediction. Instructions alone to think analytically may not change what is done.
agent_relevance: A prompt that only says 'think carefully' may not change behaviour; mode change needs a structural step, not an instruction (consistent with schema G1).

source: Barr (2014 thesis, Univ. Waterloo) Reasoned connections: complex creativity and dual-process theories of cognition
finding: Individual differences (Exp 5): disposition to engage Type 2 thinking is positively associated with success at remote analogies and the RAT, not with faith in intuition. Barr separates this 'complex creativity' from plain divergent thought; fluency was unrelated to the cognitive tasks.
numbers: N=102. Cross-domain analogies 63.7% (SD 18.8) vs within 93.8% (SD 6.3), t=17.47. RAT mean 37.6% (SD 21.4). Fluency mean 8.2 uses (SD 3.4). Originality was related to crystallised ability, not clearly to analytic style (p=.16). Exact correlation coefficients not extracted.
limits: Correlational; individual-differences design; thesis form (journal article: Barr et al. 2015, Thinking & Reasoning 21, 61-75). Smeekens & Kane (2016) are cited by Barr (2018) as pointing the other way.
agent_relevance: Different outputs depend on different resources. Single-answer reasoning tasks lean on deliberate processing; fluency does not.

source: Ellamil, Dobson, Beeman & Christoff (2012) Evaluative and generative modes of thought during the creative process, NeuroImage 59(2) 1783-94
finding: fMRI with participants designing book-cover illustrations, alternating generating and evaluating. Generation mainly engaged the medial temporal lobe; evaluation engaged executive and default network regions plus rostrolateral PFC, insula and temporopolar cortex. Executive and default regions stayed positively connected through the task.
numbers: N and effect sizes not in the abstract page I read. 291 citations (Europe PMC).
limits: Abstract only. Drawing task; N unknown from my read.
agent_relevance: Evaluation is not a single cold, rule-like process; it co-recruits spontaneous, affective processes. Judge steps may need different framing from verification steps.

source: Concordia group (2021) EEG signals respond differently to idea generation, idea evolution and evaluation in a loosely controlled creativity experiment, Scientific Reports
finding: Modified figural Torrance task with three modes: generate (first sketch), evolve (a radically different sketch), evaluate (rate difficulty). Alpha power fell from rest in all three. The lower-alpha drop was smaller in idea evolution; the upper-alpha drop was larger in evaluation than in evolution.
numbers: N=28 analysed (24 men, 4 women, ages 22-35), 29 recruited, up to 3-minute response windows.
limits: Small, mostly male graduate-student sample; modes are task-instructed, not spontaneous. EEG microstate analysis is exploratory.
agent_relevance: Three states (generate, push-further, evaluate) can be told apart physiologically. Fits a graph with an explicit 'evolve away from first idea' operator separate from judging.

source: Dynamic cycles between idea generation and evaluation during creative storytelling (2024 preprint), bioRxiv 10.1101/2024.09.04.611311
finding: fMRI brain-state analysis during story creation found more transitions between a whole-brain synchrony state (read as generation) and a control/default/visual/limbic state (read as evaluation) in creative than uncreative conception. A neural-network comparison favoured alternating over parallel operation.
numbers: N=41 (47 recruited), 20 s conception. Creative vs uncreative story rating t=13.01. State 2 to 3 transitions t=14.99, p=5.26e-8. Alternating model beat parallel: p=1.39e-32 and 2.39e-47. State 3 dwell-time difference predicted creative writing and RAT scores.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed, exploratory; state labels inferred from the literature; text-feature differences may confound; sample is Chinese college students. I read about 100,000 of 135,000 characters.
agent_relevance: Support for alternation (serial) over parallel running. A coded loop that alternates generate and judge phases is not contradicted.

source: Reflection enhances creativity: beneficial effects of idea evaluation on idea generation (2016) Brain and Cognition
finding: Alternative Uses task with EEG. Ideas generated after a phase of mentally evaluating earlier ideas were more original than after a distraction task. Evaluation came with frontal upper-alpha (10-13 Hz) synchronisation, also higher during later generation.
numbers: N and effect sizes not in the abstract page I read.
limits: Abstract only. Evaluation here is reflective review, not a score.
agent_relevance: Interleaving a judging pass raised later originality in humans. A judge-then-regenerate cycle is plausible, but the judge must sit in a separate step (G5).

source: Dual-process contributions to creativity in jazz improvisations: an SPM-EEG study (2020) NeuroImage 116632
finding: Better jazz improvisations showed more high-frequency (beta/gamma) activity over left posterior regions; poorer ones showed right temporo-parietal and fronto-polar activity. After controlling for experience, quality tracked right frontal activity. Authors read it as reduced frontal control with expertise.
numbers: N=32 jazz guitarists, 64-channel EEG, expert ratings of creativity.
limits: Abstract only. Domain-specific (music), experts; the hypofrontality reading is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Experts need less explicit control. For a model, the cheap mode may suffice once a pattern is mastered; do not force slow checks everywhere.

source: Nguyen, Tschiatschek & Singla (2025-26) Enhancing diversity of LLM-generated educational tasks (CreativeDC), arXiv 2512.23601v2
finding: Two-stage prompt inspired by divergent-convergent thinking: first explore many creative ideas, then satisfy the task requirements. Against plain and step-by-step prompting on Python task generation, it gave about 1.6 times as many distinct high-utility tasks.
numbers: Qwen3-235B-A22B, temperature 1.0. At K=50 tasks: about 13 distinct (12 high-utility) vs about 8 for both baselines (Vendi score, p<0.001, Bonferroni Wilcoxon). Three experts formed about 16 clusters vs 9. Novelty win rate 96.67% vs 3.33%; interestingness 0.81 vs 0.50; task validity 1.00 vs 0.78.
limits: One model, one domain (intro Python), 3 experts who each rated a different themed subset, so no inter-rater measure. Both stages sit in one prompt, so the model does the switch, not code. Authors list an iterated loop as future work.
agent_relevance: Closest direct LLM test of generate-then-converge. A phase split raised diversity without losing utility. Our version puts the switch in code with a real check.

source: Chavez-Autor (2025) Artificial creativity: from predictive AI to Generative System 3, Frontiers in AI
finding: Conceptual architecture: a high-entropy generator (DMN-like), a learned critic (CEN-like) and an adaptive gain controller that moves sampling entropy up or down with a performance-surprise signal. Defines update rules (exponential, linear, logistic) and proposed indices (associative-distance density, analytic-verification ratio, convergence latency).
numbers: No experiments. Proposes tasks, ablations and pass-fail criteria. Cites Doshi & Hauser (2024) for LLM output homogenisation at scale.
limits: Proposal paper with no measured results; brain-model analogy declared functional only. A learned critic would carry the model's own biases (G5).
agent_relevance: Gives a design to compare against: temperature as the mode dial. Our schema sets the mode by code from checks, not a learned gain; the GS-3 proposal is untested.

source: Al Rabeyah, Goes, Volpe & Medeiros (2025) Do LLMs agree on the creativity evaluation of alternative uses? ICCC 2025
finding: Four LLMs scored and ranked Alternative Uses responses of three known creativity levels. They agreed with each other and with an oracle ordering, and did not favour their own outputs.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash. Spearman agreement among models above 0.7 on average; above 0.77 against the oracle. 5 alternative uses per level per object.
limits: The oracle ordering was built from model-generated uses of requested creativity levels, so it is easy to rank; one task. Does not show the judge picks well among near-equal ideas.
agent_relevance: A model judge can separate common from highly creative ideas fairly well on this task. It does not remove the need for code-side checks on correctness.

source: Sen et al. (2026) Automated creativity evaluation of language models across open-ended tasks, arXiv 2606.11762
finding: Divergent creativity (semantic entropy of reasoning steps) and convergent creativity (task fulfilment by a retrieval-based multi-agent judge) are empirically separable in LLMs: correlations are weak across models and domains. Convergent score improves with model size and recency; divergent breadth does not.
numbers: Three domains: MacGyver, HypoGen, BookMIA. Models include GPT-4o and Qwen-3 variants. The judge matches individual human annotators at over 60% lower cost than prior multi-agent frameworks (authors' claim).
limits: Convergent scores come from an LLM judge, so the correlation inherits its biases (authors say so). Preprint. I read parts of the long text, not all.
agent_relevance: Generation breadth and fulfilment can be set independently. Supports tuning the two modes with separate dials, which a code-driven loop allows.

source: Divergent creativity in humans and large language models (2024-25), arXiv 2405.13012
finding: Using the Divergent Association Task from about 100,000 humans plus creative-writing tests, some LLMs beat average human DAT scores and approach human creative writing, but the best LLMs are still surpassed by highly creative people.
numbers: About 100,000 human participants (from abstract). Model list and scores not read.
limits: Abstract page only. Does not test a two-mode design.
agent_relevance: Baseline: model generation breadth is around the human average. A mode split may be needed to reach the upper tail.
